points.title: 了 — change of state
points.explain: 了 at the end of a sentence shows that something has changed or a new situation is now true. It often follows adjectives, 不 or 是 + noun. Don't confuse it with 了 right after a verb, which marks a finished action.

examples.en: I don't want to go anymore.

points.title: 快要 / 就要…了 — about to happen
points.pattern: 快要 / 就要 + Verb + 了
points.explain: 快要…了 and 就要…了 say that something will happen very soon. 就要 can follow a time word (明天就要…了), but 快要 cannot. Don't forget the 了 at the end.

examples.en: The train is about to leave.
He's going back to his country soon.

points.title: 已经…了 — already
points.explain: 已经 goes before the verb or adjective to say something has already happened. The sentence usually ends with 了. The negative is 还没…(呢), not 已经不.

points.title: 刚 / 刚才 — just now
points.explain: 刚 is an adverb right before the verb, meaning 'just'. 刚才 is a time word meaning 'a moment ago' and can go before or after the subject. 刚 can never go before the subject.

examples.en: What did you say just now?

points.title: 过 — past experience
points.explain: 过 after a verb says you have had this experience at some time in the past. It focuses on the experience, not on when it happened. Put 过 directly after the verb, before the object.

points.title: 没…过 — never done
points.explain: To say you have never done something, put 没 or 没有 before the verb and keep 过 after it. Don't use 不 here. 还没…过 means 'haven't yet'.

examples.en: He has never had Chinese food.
I've never flown on a plane yet.

points.title: 着 — continuing state
points.explain: 着 after a verb shows a state that continues, like a door being open or someone wearing something. Verb1 + 着 + Verb2 means doing Verb2 in that manner. It describes a state, not an action in progress like 正在.

examples.en: There is a book lying on the table.

points.title: 正在…呢 — action in progress
points.pattern: 正在 / 正 / 在 + Verb (+ 呢)
points.explain: 正在 (or 正, 在) before a verb shows an action happening at this moment; 呢 at the end adds a conversational tone. Don't use it with verbs that don't last, such as 知道 or 认识. Negate with 没(有).

points.title: 比 — comparison
points.explain: Put 比 between the two things you compare, then the adjective. Don't put 很 or 非常 before the adjective; use 更 or 还 if you want 'even more'.

examples.en: This one is cheaper than that one.

points.title: 比…一点儿 / 多了 — how much more
points.pattern: A + 比 + B + Adj + 一点儿 / 多了 / amount
points.explain: After the adjective in a 比 sentence you can say how big the difference is: 一点儿 (a little), 多了 or 得多 (much), or an exact amount. The difference always comes after the adjective, never before it.

examples.en: He's a little taller than me.
Today is much colder than yesterday.
My brother is three years older than me.
This one is much more expensive than that one.

points.title: 没有 — not as … as
points.pattern: A + 没有 + B + (那么) + Adj
points.short: A is not as … as B
points.explain: A 没有 B + adjective means A doesn't reach B's level. You can add 那么 or 这么 before the adjective. Don't use 不比 for this; it means something slightly different.

examples.en: I'm not as tall as him.
Today isn't as hot as yesterday.
It's not as cold here as in Beijing.
My Chinese isn't as good as yours.

points.title: 跟…一样 — the same as
points.pattern: A + 跟 / 和 + B + 一样 (+ Adj)
points.short: A is the same as B
points.explain: 跟…一样 says two things are the same; add an adjective after 一样 to say in what way. 和 can replace 跟. The negative is 跟…不一样.

examples.en: My book is the same as yours.
He is as tall as his dad.
Today is as cold as yesterday.
This one is different from that one.

points.title: 不如 — not as good as
points.explain: A 不如 B means A is not as good as B. You can add an adjective at the end to say in what way. Without an adjective, it simply means 'worse than'.

examples.en: My handwriting isn't as good as his.
Taking a car isn't as fast as walking.
This one isn't as good as that one.
Today's food isn't as good as yesterday's.

points.title: 更 — even more
points.explain: 更 means 'even more' and implies a comparison with something already mentioned. It goes before adjectives or verbs like 喜欢. Unlike 很, it always compares.

points.title: 越来越 — more and more
points.explain: 越来越 shows that something keeps increasing over time. Put it right before the adjective or verb, and don't add 很. The sentence often ends with 了.

examples.en: His Chinese is getting better and better.
Things are getting more and more expensive.
I like Beijing more and more.

points.title: 会 — know how to
points.explain: 会 means you have learned how to do something, like a language, driving or cooking. For physical ability or permission use 能 or 可以 instead. Negate with 不会.

points.title: 会 — will probably
points.explain: 会 can also predict that something is likely to happen. Adding 的 at the end makes it sound more certain. The negative 不会 means 'won't'.

points.title: 能 — be able to
points.explain: 能 says someone is able to do something, or that conditions allow it. Use 会 for learned skills but 能 for capacity, e.g. how much you can do. Negate with 不能.

examples.en: He can write 100 characters a day.
I'm sick and can't go to class.

points.title: 可以 — may, allowed
points.explain: 可以 asks for or gives permission. 可以 alone works as a short 'yes' answer. To refuse, people often say 不行 or 不能.

points.title: 要 — want to, going to
points.explain: 要 + verb shows a strong wish or a plan: 'want to', 'be going to'. It is stronger than 想. To say 'don't want to', use 不想, because 不要 means 'don't!'.

examples.en: I'm going to China next year.
What do you want to buy?
He's going to learn to drive.

points.title: 想 — would like to
points.explain: 想 + verb expresses a wish: 'would like to', 'feel like'. It is softer and more polite than 要. Negate with 不想.

examples.en: I'd like to rest a bit.
What would you like to eat?
I'd like to go see a movie.
I don't feel like going to work.

points.title: 应该 — should
points.explain: 应该 gives advice or says what is right to do. It goes before the verb. The negative is 不应该, 'shouldn't'.

examples.en: We should leave a bit earlier.

points.title: 得 / 必须 — must, have to
points.explain: 得 (pronounced děi) is spoken Chinese for 'have to'; 必须 is stronger and more formal. The negative is 不用 ('don't have to'), never 不得 or 不必须.

examples.en: You have to get up early tomorrow.
You must go to the hospital.

points.title: 不用 — no need to
points.explain: 不用 means 'there is no need to'. It's the negative of 得 and 要 when they mean 'have to'. 不用谢 and 不用客气 are polite set phrases.

examples.en: You don't need to buy a ticket.
You don't need to wait for me.

points.title: 别 / 不要 — don't!
points.explain: 别 and 不要 before a verb tell someone not to do something. 别 is more casual. Adding 了 at the end (别…了) means 'stop doing it'.

points.title: 就 — early, quickly
points.explain: 就 before the verb shows the speaker feels something happens early, quickly or easily. The time word comes before 就. These sentences often end with 了.

examples.en: He got up as early as six.
We got there in just ten minutes.

points.title: 才 — late, only then
points.explain: 才 before the verb shows the speaker feels something happens late or takes a long time. Unlike 就, 才 sentences usually don't end with 了.

examples.en: He didn't get up until ten.
Why are you only coming now?

examples.text: 我等了一个小时他才来。
examples.en: I waited an hour before he came.
He didn't get home until eight.

points.title: 因为…所以 — because… so
points.explain: 因为 introduces the reason and 所以 the result. You can use both or just one of them. 因为 can also come in the second half to give the reason afterwards.

examples.en: Because it rained, I didn't go.

examples.text: 因为他病了，所以没来上课。
examples.en: He was sick, so he didn't come to class.

examples.text: 因为很忙，所以他没吃午饭。
examples.en: He was busy, so he skipped lunch.
I didn't go because I was sick.

points.title: 虽然…但是 — although… but
points.pattern: 虽然 + A，但是 / 可是 + B
points.explain: 虽然 introduces a fact and 但是 or 可是 introduces a contrasting result. Unlike English, Chinese normally uses both words together. 虽然 can go before or after the subject.

examples.text: 虽然很累，但是我很高兴。
虽然汉语很难，但是很有意思。
examples.en: Chinese is hard, but it's interesting.

examples.text: 这件衣服虽然贵，但是很好看。
examples.en: This is pricey, but it looks great.

examples.text: 他虽然很忙，可是每天都运动。
examples.en: Though busy, he exercises every day.

points.title: 如果…就 — if… then
points.pattern: 如果 + condition (+ 的话)，就 + result
points.explain: 如果 introduces a condition and 就 goes before the verb of the result. 的话 at the end of the condition is optional, and you can even drop 如果 and keep only 的话. 就 must come after the subject, not before it.

examples.text: 如果明天下雨，我就不去了。
examples.en: If it rains tomorrow, I won't go.

examples.text: 如果你有时间，就来我家吧。
examples.en: If you have time, come to my place.

examples.text: 如果你累了，就休息一下。
examples.en: If you're tired, take a rest.

examples.text: 你不想去的话，就别去了。
examples.en: If you don't want to go, then don't.

points.title: 不但…而且 — not only… but also
points.explain: 不但…而且 adds a second, often stronger point to the first. If both parts share a subject, put it before 不但. 而且 can also be used alone to mean 'and also'.

examples.text: 这个菜不但好吃，而且便宜。
examples.en: This dish is tasty and cheap too.

examples.text: 她不但漂亮，而且很热情。
examples.en: She's not only pretty but also warm.

examples.text: 他不但会唱歌，而且会画画儿。
examples.en: He can sing and paint too.

examples.text: 今天不但冷，而且下雪了。
examples.en: It's not only cold today, it's snowing.

points.title: 一边…一边 — while
points.pattern: 一边 + Verb1 + 一边 + Verb2
points.explain: 一边…一边 links two actions done at the same time by the same person. Each 一边 goes right before a verb. Don't use it for states like 高兴 or 累.

examples.text: 他一边吃饭一边看电视。
不要一边开车一边打电话。

points.title: 先…再 / 然后 — first… then
points.pattern: 先 + A，再 / 然后 + B
points.explain: 先 marks the first action and 再 or 然后 the next one. 再 goes right before the verb, while 然后 starts the second clause. They are often combined: 然后再….

examples.en: I'll wash my hands first, then eat.

examples.text: 我们先去商店，然后回家。
examples.en: We'll go to the store, then home.

points.title: 又…又 — both… and
points.explain: 又…又 describes two qualities or actions at the same time. Both parts should be positive or both negative. Put each 又 right before the adjective or verb.

examples.en: This dish is both tasty and cheap.

points.title: 还是 — or (questions)
points.explain: 还是 asks someone to choose between options. It's used in questions, so don't add 吗 at the end. For 'or' in statements, use 或者.

examples.en: Would you like tea or water?
Are you going today or tomorrow?
Do you want rice or noodles?

points.title: 或者 — or (statements)
points.explain: 或者 means 'or' in statements, when either choice is fine. It is not used for choice questions; those use 还是. It often appears with 都可以 or 都行.

examples.en: Tomorrow or the day after is fine.
You can have tea or milk.

examples.text: 周末我看书或者看电影。
examples.en: On weekends I read or watch movies.

examples.text: 打电话或者发短信都行。
examples.en: A call or a text is fine.

points.title: 再 — again (future)
points.explain: 再 means 'again' or 'once more' for actions that haven't happened yet. It also means 'then, later' as in 明天再说. For repeats that already happened, use 又.

examples.en: I'd like to eat one more.

points.title: 又 — again (already happened)
points.explain: 又 means 'again' for something that has already happened once more. The sentence often ends with 了. For future repetition, use 再 instead.

examples.text: 昨天下雨，今天又下雨了。
examples.en: It rained yesterday and again today.

points.title: 还 — still, also
points.explain: 还 means 'still' (something continues) or 'also, in addition'. 还没 means 'not yet'. 还要 means 'also want / still need'.

examples.en: I also want to buy a book.

points.title: 有点儿 + Adj — a bit (too)
points.explain: 有点儿 before an adjective means 'a bit', usually for something unpleasant. It goes before the adjective. Don't confuse it with 一点儿, which comes after the adjective.

points.title: Adj + 一点儿 — a bit more
points.explain: 一点儿 after an adjective means 'a little more …', used for requests and comparisons. It comes after the adjective, unlike 有点儿. In speech it is often shortened to 点儿.

examples.en: This one is a bit bigger.

points.title: 一点儿也不 — not at all
points.pattern: 一点儿 + 也 / 都 + 不 / 没 + …
points.explain: 一点儿也不 + adjective or verb means 'not at all'. 都 can replace 也. For the past, use 没 instead of 不.

examples.en: He doesn't want to go at all.
I didn't eat anything at all.

points.title: Verb + 完 — finish
points.explain: 完 after a verb means the action is finished. Negate it with 没: 没吃完. Remember 完 attaches to the verb, not to the object.

examples.en: Have you finished reading this book?

points.title: Verb + 到 — reach, succeed
points.explain: 到 after a verb shows the action reached its goal: you found, got, or arrived. Negate with 没: 没买到 means you tried but didn't get it. It also marks reaching a place: 走到.

points.title: 看见 / 听见 — perceive
points.explain: 看 and 听 are actions (look, listen); adding 见 shows you actually perceived something. Negate with 没: 没看见. 看到 and 听到 mean the same.

points.title: Verb + 好 — done properly
points.explain: 好 after a verb means the action is done well or completely, so something is ready. It's common with 做, 准备, 想 and 坐. Negate with 没.

points.title: Verb + 错 / 对 — wrong or right
points.explain: 错 after a verb says the action was done wrongly; 对 says it was done correctly. Common examples are 写错, 说对, 听错, 打错. Negate with 没.

points.title: Verb + 懂 / 清楚 — understand
points.explain: 懂 after 听 or 看 means you understood what you heard or read. 清楚 means clearly. Negate with 没: 我没听懂.

points.title: 得 / 不 — can or can't (result)
points.explain: Put 得 between a verb and its result to say it is possible, or 不 to say it is impossible. 听不懂 means 'can't understand'; 听得懂 means 'can understand'. It is used much more in the negative.

points.title: 来 / 去 — direction
points.explain: 来 after a verb means movement toward the speaker; 去 means away from the speaker. A place word goes before 来/去: 回家去. Choose by where the speaker is.

points.title: Compound direction — 走进来 / 拿出去
points.pattern: Verb + 进/出/上/下/回/过 + 来/去
points.explain: A verb can take two direction words: the first shows the path (进, 出, 上, 下, 回, 过), the second (来/去) the direction relative to the speaker. An object often goes between them or before 来/去.

examples.text: 他从包里拿出来一本书。
examples.en: He took a book out of his bag.

points.title: Verb + 得 + Adj — how well
points.short: how well an action is done
points.explain: 得 after a verb introduces a comment on how the action is done. The adjective usually takes 很 or another adverb. Negate the adjective, not the verb: 说得不好.

points.title: Verb + Obj + Verb + 得 — with object
points.explain: When the verb has an object, repeat the verb before 得: 说汉语说得很好. You can also drop the first verb: 他汉语说得很好. Don't say 说汉语得很好.

examples.en: I'm not good at ball games.

points.title: 把 — do something to an object
points.explain: 把 moves the object before the verb to stress what is done to it. The verb can't stand alone: it needs something after it, like 完, 好, 了 or a place. The object must be something specific.

examples.en: Put the book on the table.

points.title: 给 + person + Verb — for, to
points.explain: 给 + person before the verb says who receives or benefits from the action. It's common with 打电话, 写信, 买. Put 给 + person before the verb, not after.

points.title: 给 / 送 / 教 — two objects
points.explain: Verbs like 给, 送, 教, 告诉 and 问 can take two objects: first the person, then the thing. Don't add a word like 'to' between them.

points.title: 离 — distance from
points.pattern: A + 离 + B + 远 / 近
points.short: distance from a place or time
points.explain: 离 tells the distance between two places or until a time. Use it with 远, 近, or 还有 + time. Don't use 从 for this; 从 marks a starting point.

examples.en: My home is close to school.
Is the airport far from here?
Is your home far from here?
Three days left until the exam.

points.title: 从…到… — from… to…
points.explain: 从…到… marks a starting and ending point in place or time. The whole phrase goes before the verb. 从 alone means 'from'.

examples.text: 从我家到学校要十分钟。
examples.en: It's ten minutes from home to school.

examples.text: 我从八点到十二点上课。
examples.en: I have class from eight to twelve.
Is it far from here to the airport?
He works from morning till night.

points.title: 往 / 向 — toward
points.explain: 往 and 向 + a direction or place show which way an action goes. They come before the verb. 向 can also be used with people: 向我走来.

points.title: 对 — to, toward
points.explain: 对 introduces the person or thing an attitude or effect is directed at: 对我很好 'kind to me'. 对…好 also means 'good for'. Put the 对-phrase before the adjective or verb.

examples.en: The teacher is warm to the students.
Exercise is good for your health.

points.title: 跟…一起 — together with
points.pattern: 跟 / 和 + person + 一起 + Verb
points.explain: 跟…一起 or 和…一起 says you do something together with someone. The phrase goes before the verb. 一起 alone means 'together'.

examples.text: 周末我跟妈妈一起买东西。
examples.en: I shop with Mom on weekends.

points.title: Verb + duration — how long
points.explain: The length of time goes after the verb, not before it. The object comes after the time phrase: 学了两年汉语. With 了 it describes a finished period.

examples.en: I studied Chinese for two years.
I waited for him for half an hour.

points.title: Verb + 次 / 遍 — how many times
points.explain: 次 counts how many times something happens; 遍 counts complete times through something from start to end. The number + 次/遍 goes after the verb.

examples.en: I've been to Beijing three times.
I take medicine three times a day.
He has been to my house once.

points.title: Verb reduplication — 看看
points.explain: Doubling a verb makes the action short, light or casual, and makes requests softer. Two-syllable verbs double as ABAB: 休息休息. Don't double verbs like 是 or 有.

examples.en: Have a look at this book.
I'd like to try on this.

points.title: Verb + 一下 — briefly
points.explain: 一下 after a verb means doing it briefly or once, and makes a request sound polite. It's very common in 等一下, 看一下, 介绍一下. The object goes after 一下.

examples.text: 我介绍一下，这是我朋友。
examples.en: Let me introduce: this is my friend.
Could you help me a moment?

points.title: …的时候 — when
points.explain: …的时候 turns a clause into a time phrase: 'when …'. It comes before the main clause, unlike English 'when' which can come at the end.

examples.en: I don't talk when I eat.
When he came, I was sleeping.
Don't play on your phone in class.

examples.text: 我在中国的时候学了汉语。
examples.en: I learned Chinese while in China.

points.title: 以前 / 以后 — before / after
points.explain: 以前 and 以后 come after the event or time, the opposite of English 'before'/'after'. Alone at the start of a sentence they mean 'in the past' and 'in the future'.

examples.en: After class I'll go to the library.
I didn't use to like sports.

points.title: 是…的 — stressing details
points.explain: 是…的 emphasizes when, where, how or with whom a past action happened. The detail goes right after 是, and 的 comes at the end. 是 can be dropped in speech, but 的 cannot.

points.title: Measure words — 件 / 条 / 只 / 辆
points.pattern: Number / 这 / 那 + measure word + Noun
points.short: special measure words (件, 条, 只…)
points.explain: Many nouns have their own measure word: 件 for clothes and matters, 条 for long things, 只 for many animals, 辆 for vehicles. Use 个 only when you're unsure; the right one sounds much more natural.

examples.en: I bought a piece of clothing.

points.title: 几 / 多 — approximate numbers
points.pattern: 十几 / 二十多 / 一个多小时
points.explain: 几 means 'a few' (under ten), as in 十几 'a dozen or so'. 多 after a round number means 'more than'. With a measure word, 多 goes before it for numbers ending in 0, but after it for 一个多小时.

examples.en: Our class has a dozen or so people.

points.title: 每…都 — every
points.pattern: 每 + measure word + Noun + 都 + Verb
points.explain: 每 means 'every' and needs a measure word (每个人, 每次), except with 天 and 年. It is usually paired with 都 before the verb.

points.title: 一…就 — as soon as
points.explain: 一…就 means that B happens right after A, or every time A happens. 一 and 就 both go right before verbs, after the subjects.

examples.en: I slept as soon as I got home.
He gets sleepy whenever he reads.
When it's hot, I don't want to eat.
I got it as soon as the teacher explained.

points.title: 什么都 / 谁都 — anything, anyone
points.pattern: Question word + 都 / 也 + Verb
points.explain: A question word + 都 or 也 means 'every' or, in negative sentences, 'any': 什么都吃 'eats everything', 哪儿都不去 'go nowhere'. The question word comes before the verb.

examples.en: I don't want to go anywhere.

points.title: 多 + Adj？— how (big, far…)
points.pattern: 多 + 大 / 远 / 高 / 久？
points.explain: 多 before an adjective asks about degree: 多大 'how old/big', 多远 'how far', 多久 'how long'. Only positive adjectives are used this way, so ask 多高, not 多矮.

examples.en: How far is your home from here?
How long have you studied Chinese?

points.title: 这么 / 那么 — so (this/that much)
points.pattern: 这么 / 那么 + Adj / Verb
points.explain: 这么 and 那么 before an adjective mean 'so …' and add emotion or surprise. 这么 refers to something near or present, 那么 to something far away or mentioned before.

examples.en: Why is it so cold today?
Why did you buy so much?

points.title: 好像 — seems
points.explain: 好像 means 'it seems' or 'looks like' and shows you're not completely sure. It goes before the verb or at the start of the sentence.

examples.en: It looks like it's raining outside.
I think I've met you before.

points.title: 可能 — maybe
points.explain: 可能 as an adverb means 'maybe, probably'. It goes before the verb or at the start. It can combine with 会: 可能会下雨.

examples.en: What you said may be right.

points.title: 一定 — definitely
points.explain: 一定 shows certainty: 'definitely, surely'. With your own plans it's a promise; about others it's a confident guess. 一定要 means 'must be sure to'.

points.title: 让 — let, make someone
points.explain: 让 means 'let', 'have' or 'make' someone do something or feel something. The person comes right after 让, then the verb. 让我… is a common way to offer: 'let me…'.

examples.en: Mom told me to sleep early.
The teacher had us read the text.
Don't make him wait for me.

points.title: 只 — only
points.explain: 只 means 'only' and goes before the verb, not before the noun. 只能 means 'can only'. So say 我只有十块钱, not 我有只十块钱.

points.title: 还是…吧 — had better
points.explain: 还是…吧 gives a suggestion after thinking about options: 'you'd better…'. Here 还是 doesn't mean 'or'. 吧 at the end softens it.

examples.en: It's late; let's take a taxi.

examples.text: 你病了，还是在家休息吧。
examples.en: You're sick; better rest at home.
